*441. SHRI C. O. POULOSE: W ill the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES be pleased to state:

[23 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRIMATI 
VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) The Ministry of Small Scale Industries and Agro and 
Rural Industries has not set up such a Working Group. 
(b) and (c) Questions do not arise, in view of the above. 
SHRI CO. POULOSE: Mr. Chairman, Sir, dumping of consumer goods such as 
dry batteries, sports shoes, toys, etc., is increasing alarmingly. The threats to 
domestic units and products are being addressed through antidumping action, 
imposition of countervailing duties and safeguard measures under the relevant WTO 
agreements. An Inter-Ministerial Group, under the Chairmanship of the Commerce 
Secretary, has been constituted to assess the impact of removal of quantitative 
restrictions and suggest suitable corrective measures. This piece of information was 
given in this House in reply to theUnstarred Question No. 2232. What are the 
recommendations and the steps taken thereon? 
SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE: Sir, the question was on the setting up of a 
Working Group to formulate an approach on the small-scale industries. This has not 
happened in this Ministry. I know what the Member is referring to. He is referring to 
an Inter-Ministerial Work Group which has been set up in the Ministry of 
Commerce to monitor the position of imports. Three hundred items have been 
identified to be watched for import surges, after the removal of QRs. Out of these, 
sixty seven items are belonging to the SSIs. Regarding these 300 (items, the two-
month data shows that there was a growth of -11 % Regarding the 67 SSI items, the 
provisional data of imports shows a growth of 5.59% during 2000-2001, while the 
exports grew at the rate of 26.39%. 
SHRI C. O. POULOSE: Sir, my second supplementary is that after the 
announcement of the policy package to strengthen the small-scale sector on 30th 
August, 2000, which includes easier access to credit availability of collateral free 
composite loans, capital subsidy for technological upgradation and improved 
infrastructure, out of the 55.36 lakh manufacturing units, more than 3 lakh units 
are reported to be sick. The loss of employment because of the sickness and 
closure is increasing enormously. As a result of globalisation, many commodities 
are imported to this country, which has made the continuance of these industries 
unviable. What are the steps the Government intends to take to check the ill-effects of 
recession as well as import liberalisation? 
 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2001 ] 
SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE: Sir, I would not put these two together. I 
would not say the sickness in industry is because of globalisation. But I would say here 
that the information on sickness is not maintained centrally, neither State-wise. The 
information comes to us from the RBI and it is true that in the last year the figure of 
sickness was 3,04,000. Apart from the composite package, we have taken other measures 
to deal with the sickness. The State-level Institutional Committees have been set up for 
timely identification and rehabilitation of the potentially viable sick industries. Special 
Rehabilitation Cells in banks and other State financial institutions have been set up 
and elaborate guidelines have been issued by the RBI for extending rehabilitation 
assistance to eligible units. A one-time settlement formula, the Samadhan Scheme, 
has been announced by the RBI on 27th July, 2000 for the settlement of dues. There is a 
Delayed Payment Act which provides for penal interest on delayed payments to small 
units. This has also been helpful in reducing some sickness due to delayed payments. 
Finally, as per our comprehensive policy package, we have set up a Committee to 
draw up revised guidelines for the rehabilitation of me currently sick but potentially 
viable SSI units. The RBI has already received the report of the Committee. The RBI is 
drawing up fresh guidelines. We are waiting for intimation from the RBI. I am sure it 
will help us in the early detection of sick units and timely revival of sick industries.

SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE: Sir, this is a myth that seems to be perpetuated 
time and again that the small-scale industries are in their death throes. It is not true because 
mis can be proved by the figures which have been collected over the last four years. If we 
look at these figures, in 1997-98 the industrial sector growth rate was at 6.7 per cent, while 
that of the SSI sector was at 8.43 per cent. In 1998-99, in me case of small-scale sector, it 
was 7.71 per cent and in the case of industrial sector, it was 4.1 per cent. Again in 1999-
2000, in me case of industrial secret, it was 6.5 per cent; whereas in the case of SSI 
sector it was 8.16 per cent. Now in the year 2000-01—we have provisional figures—in 
the case of industrial sector, it is 4.9 per cent and in the case of SSI sector, it has grown 
at the rate of 8.09 per cent. Sir, the SSI associations have also been invited  
4 

[23 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
to participate in whatever discussions and consultations we have had. I would not 
say that the small-scale sector is in a very bad shape. Yes, after liberalisation and 
globalisation, there is going to be a very difficult task ahead of the small-scale 
industries because they will have to face more competition. But we are looking 
towards a larger infusion of capital and technology and so also the opportunity to 
expand and reap the benefits of economies of scale which would more than 
compensate for these disadvantages. The small-scale industries will have to improve 
their quality and competitiveness in order to survive. We have taken measures to 
provide mem any kind of support in case any pressure comes upon the small-scale 
sector. I don't mink there is any need to worry on this count. The Government is 
alive to the problems of the small-scale sector. The Government will take all 
appropriate measures to give them full support.

Activities conducted by NCP 
*443. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state:  
(a) what are the main aims and obj ectives of National Commission on

(b) the activities conducted by NCP since January, 2001; 
(c) the funds allocated for the NCP during the current year; and 
(d) the achievements of NCP since its inception? 
15 

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2001 ] 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. CR 
THAKUR): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The main aims and objectives of the National Commission on 
Population are given below: 
(1) To review, monitor and give directions for the implementation of the 
National Population Policy with a view to meeting the goals set out 
in the policy. 
(2) To promote synergy between demographic, educational, 
environmental and developmental programmes so as to hasten 
population stabilization. 
(3) To promote inter-sectoral coordination in planning and 
implementation across government agencies of the Central and State 
Governments, to involve the civil society and the private sector and 
to explore the possibilities of international cooperation in support of 
the goals set out in the Policy. 
(4) To facilitate the development of a vigorous people's movement in 
support of this national effort. 
(b) and (d) Brief details of the activities/achievements of the NCP are given 
below: 
1. Review of the implementation of National Family Welfare Programme 
TJie present growth in the population of the country is basically due to 
three factors. About 60% of  the growth can be attributed to the large size of 
the population in the repr oductive age group.  This is bound to take place 
because of what has happened in the past. Another 20% of the growth in 
population is said to be due to the high unmet needs fo r contraception. The 
balance 20% is due to other socio-economic factors like high infant mortality, 
low status of women, son preference, illiteracy, poverty, etc. 
The elements of population growth amenable to policy intervention 
relate to the latter two categories, namely meeting the unmet needs for 
contraception and improving the social , economic and demographic factors 
affecting population growth. The National Population Policy (NPP) 2000 states 
that the unmet needs for basic reproductive and child health services, supplies 
and infrastructure should be met at the earliest. If the unmet needs for 
16 

[23 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
contraceptives can be met, especially in the high population growth States like Uttar 
Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh, the same could go a long way in 
reducing the overall population growth significantly. In view of the crucial role of these 
States in achieving the objectives of demographic stabilization, Vice-Chairman, 
NCP took two meetings with the Chief Secretaries/Family Welfare Secretaries of 
these States for a thorough review of the implementation of the Family Welfare 
Programmes. These reviews have helped to identify the various problems in each State 
and the remedial measures required. Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and UP have since 
brought out their separate population policy documents along with a programme of 
action for population stabilization within a time frame. Bihar is in the process of finalizing 
its population policy. The Member Secretary, NCP has also visited UP, Madhya Pradesh 
and Bihar to discuss the issues relating to population stabilization with concerned 
State Government officials. 
At the national level, the implementation of the Family Welfare 
Programmes was reviewed in a meeting taken by Vice-Chairman, NCP with Minister 
for Health and Family Welfare on 9.8.2001, in which the present level of use of 
different types of contraceptives, the couple protection rate, the financial and 
physical achievements etc. were examined and the need for a restrategisation of the 
programme was brought out. The need for drawing up area specific action plans to 
improve social, economic and demographic factors in the high fertility areas was 
emphasized. The necessity for evolving a mechanism for involving the Panchayati 
Raj Institutions, NGOs, women self-help groups and promoting public and private 
participation was brought out in order to ensure that the services reached the 
needy. 
2. Identification of high fertility districts and preparation of District Action 
Plans 
There are considerable inter-State and intra-State differences relating to 
demographic indicators. The district being the key unit in implementing various 
programmes, the NCP has undertaken an exercise to identify the high fertility 
districts in the country. This has shown that there are 133 districts having above 
3.5 Total Fertility Rate (TFR) and another 196 districts with TFR between 2.5 and 
3.5 against the NPP target of reaching replacement level TFR of 2.1 by 2010 for the 
country as a whole. After this, as a first step, the Commission convened a meeting of 
the District Magistrates of the 133 high fertility districts to understand the ground 
realities as also to sensitise them about the various issues which have a bearing on 
populatior 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2001] 
growth. After detailed discussions, the District Magistrates resolved to bring up 
population related issues upfront which involve fully meeting the unmet needs for 
reproductive and child health services so as to reach the replacement level fertility at 
the earliest. They further decided that District Action Plans would be prepared 
with short-term, medium-term and l ong-term objectives. The action plans 
prepared/being prepared will bring out the position about the infrastructure, 
human and other resources available and the existing gaps in them with a definite 
programme of action for covering these gaps within a given time frame. 
3. Selection of social, economic and demographic indicators for 
monitoring purpose 
The NCP document is noteworthy in that it transcends purely 
demographic concerns and aims at the over-riding objective of economic and 
social development to improve the quality of life of the people of India. In this 
perspective, it was also felt that the traditional ways of monitoring the progress 
in terms of financial and physical achievements might not serve the purpose in 
identifying factors leading to high population growth. Therefore, after extensive 
discussions, the NCP selected some social, economic and demographic indicators 
such as female literacy, age of marriage of girls, safe delivery for mother, child 
survival, clean drinking water supply, basic sanitation facility, child nutrition, 
immunization and adoption of family planning methods which directly or 
indirectly influence human fertility. In the light of the deliberations at the DM's 
Conference, the list of indicators were modified. Then, using the data from Census 
2001 and other sources, the NCP has ranked and mapped 569 districts of the 
country on the basis of 12 social, economic and demographic indicators and a 
composite index based on them with a view to know the comparative position of 
each district in relation to these indicators. This data was published on the occasion 
of World Population Day on 11 th July, 2001. The information/data brought out by 
this publication is useful to policy-makers, administrators, researchers and all those 
who are concerned with regional di sparities in economic and social 
development. The regular collection, analysis and publication of data relating to 
these indicators will be a major change in the strategy for monitoring the 
implementation of social sector programmes. For this purpose, a Standing 
Committee for Monitoring of the NCP has been set up with representatives of the 
concerned Central Ministries, State Governments and NGOs as recommended by the 
Task Force on Monitoring chaired by the Vice-Chairman, NCP. 
18 

[23 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
4. Conference of Demographic Research Organisations 
As envisaged in the,NPP, integration of  the results of research with policy 
formulation is important for effectively addressing various issues related to 
population stabilization. Therefore, on 20th March, 2001, the NCP convened a 
Conference of the organizations/experts involved in demographic research: This 
Conference was attended by representa tives of 19 Population Resarch Centres 
(PRCs) from all over India, Indian Institute of Management, Lucknow, Indian 
Council for Medical Research, Institute for Economic Growth, New Delhi, United 
Nations Fund for Population - Activities (UNFPA), UNICEF, noted demographers, 
NGOs and senior officers from the concerned Departments of the Government of 
India. The NCP plans to utilize the PRCs and other research organizations in 
evaluation studies of social sector programmes. Such studies have already been 
sponsored by the Commission in relation to Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. 
The proper utilization of the results of the research and evaluation studies can help 
improve the quality, reduce the cost and introduce the required changes from time 
to time in policies and programmes. 
5. The recommendations of the Working Groups constituted by the NCP 
On the basis of decisions taken at the Strategic Support Group of Secretaries 
of the concerned Departments, the NCP had constituted some Working Groups to 
examine the strategies for meeting the unmet needs for contraception, maternal, child 
and public health, empowerment of women, development of children, drinking water, 
nutrition, sanitation, issues relating to adolescents, main streaming of the Indian 
system of medicine, tribal communities, monitoring and media for information, 
education and communication. Most of these Groups have already completed their work 
and submitted their recommendations/reports. These are being integrated to the extent 
possible in the policies and programees for the 10th Five Year Plan. The programme of 
action emerging out of these recommendations will also be considered in separate 
meetings with each of the concerned Ministries at the Centre and the States. 
6. Evolving grass-root level models 
The NPP document mentions that Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) are important 
for furthering decentralized planning and programme implementation. It also states 
that population stabilization efforts will be effective only if an integrated package of 
essential services are reached at the village 
19 

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2001] 
and household levels. Presently, many of the services and programmes of social 
sectors are not reaching the people at th e village level in the desired manner. 
There is also a multiplicit y of agencies and employ ees representing different 
departments working in the rural areas in an uncoordinated manner. Because of 
uiis, there is a need to think about alternative for ensuring better delivery of 
services and supplies at the village level and for maintenance of the infrastructure 
facilities in sectors like health, family welfare and education. For this purpose, 
the active involvement of elected representatives of PRIs, NGOs and village 
self-help groups active at the grass-root level is important. In an effort to develop 
appropriate models/strategies and to understand innovative policies and 
programmes being implemented in some places, the NCP has organized field 
visits to some of the village Panchayats in high fertility areas. Some members of 
the Commission and representatives of the national level NGOs also participated 
in these visits, which may help evolve alternative strategies for meeting the 
unmet needs relating to different social sectors in the rural areas. Points for 
action which emerged out of these visits include control and supervision of all 
village level functionaries by PRIs, training programmes for women members 
of PRIs, self-help groups, etc. to improve their awareness and empowerment, 
involving the practitioners of Indian System of Medicine and Homeopathy to 
fill the gaps in human resources, coordinating the functioning of all social 
sector field level workers and adoption of contract system of employment with 
performance related incentives for field level employees. The involvement of 
PRIs and village level organizations can help preparation of Panchayat Action 
Plans to address specific issues rela ting to population stabilization in each 
Panchayat/village. To help operationalise the District Action Plans, the Panchayat 
Action Plans are also being encouraged.

crores.

*444. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the

(a) Whether the thermometers used for measuring body temperature now

thermometers find dieir way to me chemist shops across die country; and

manufacturers get ISI standardisation mark on die product tfiey put for sale in the

THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHANTA KUMAR): (a) There have been reports that 
some of the clinical thermometers available in the market are inaccurate and/or

(b) The Standards of Weights & Measures Act 1976 provides that 
24 

[23 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
every unit of weight or measures shall be based on the metric system. 
Thermometers are, therefore, to be marked only in degree Celsius. Most of the 
manufacturers, however, have been making thermometers with Fahrenheit 
marking or dual marking, i.e. with degree Fahrenheit and Celsius. Manufacture, 
sale and use of such non-standard thermometers amounts to contravention of the 
Standards of Weights & Measures Act, 1976 and the Standards of Weights & 
Measures (Enforcement) Act, 1985. Such non-standard thermometers are, 
therefore, not submitted by the manufacturers for verification by the Weights & 
Measures enforcement authorities in the States. Enforcement authorities in some 
States are carrying out inspections of retail shops to check the sale of non-standard 
thermometers and launching prosecution in suitable cases. 
(c) Government propose to take action under the Bureau of Indian Standards 
(BIS) Act, 1986 to direct the use of the BIS standard mark under a license as 
compulsory for enclosed scale and solid stem type clinical thermometers to 
ensure that such thermometers manufactured and sold in the market meet the 
requirements of the Weights & Measures laws and also conform to the quality 
standards prescribed by BIS.

Job Opportunities for Industrial Labour 
*449. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the causes of the present slump in job market for industrial labour in the 
country; 
(b) the details of the measures taken by Government, recently, in regard to 
improvements in job opportunities for industrial labour; 
(c) whether Government have taken note of the recommendations of the 
Montek Singh Committee in this regard; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the measures taken by Government to implement the 
recommendations and ease slump in job market and eliminate present 
sufferings of the industrial labour? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (DR. SATYA NARAYAN JATIYA): (a) to (e) 
The main reasons for not achieving the desired growth rate of employment for 
industrial labour in the country are as follows: 
1. Present rate of economic growth not being in tune with the 
requirements for employment generation. 
2. Employment opportunities in the old industries are getting reduced due to 
closer of older type of enterprises. 
29 

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2001] 
3. Old technologies are getting replaced by new technologies, the 
demand for unskilled and semi-skilled workers are less. Skilled 
labour are more in demand in these new industries. 
4. In the present scenario, the employment rate has come down since the 
average skill level of the workers is not in tune with demand of the 
labour market. 
In order to cope up with the situation indicated above, Government is 
revising the courses run by Industrial Training Institutes. At the same time, new 
trades are being introduced as per the demand of the market. Same procedure is 
followed for Apprenticeship Training Programmes. The Advanced Training 
Institutes under Ministry of Labour is running courses for upgradation of the 
skill level of the workers already employed. 
The report of the Task Force under the Chairmanship of Dr. Montek Singh 
Ahluwalia has been received. The sports suggested generation of employment 
through intervention in 5 major areas as follows: 
* Accelerating the rate of growth of GDP, with a particular emphasis on 
sectors likely to ensure the spread of income to the low income 
segments of the labour force. 
* Pursuing appropriate sectoral policies in individual sectors which are 
particularly important for employment generation. These sector level 
policies must be broadly consistent with the overall objective of 
accelerating GDP growth. 
* Implementing focused special programmes for creating additional 
employment of enhancing income generation from existing activities 
aimed at helping vulnerable groups that may not be sufficiently 
benefited by the move general growth promoting policies. 
* Pursuing suitable policies for education and skill development, which 
would upgrade the quality of the labour force and make it capable of 
supporting a growth process which geneates high quality jobs. 
The above report is being analysed and further action will be taken as per 
the decision of die Government on it.

Delegation to enquire into rejection of wheat by Iraq 
3362. SHRI CO. POULOSE: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a delegation was sent to meet Iraqi officials in order to find out 
why the shipments of Indian wheat was first found substandard there and later fit in 
Dubai; and 
(b) if so, what are their findings? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM 
CHAUHAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Indian wheat was not substandard and conformed to the CODEX 
Standards. As per the International CODEX standards, foreign matter in the 
grain is permissible upto 2%, out of which 1.5% may consist of organic matter, 
such as chaff, weed seed, other edible and inedible grains, etc. and the balance 
0.5% inorganic foreign matter, such as stones, sand, dust etc. Quality specification 
prescribed in the Iraqi contract provided for the presence 
of foreign matter upto 2%. There was no further break-up of this 2% into organic 
and inorganic foreign matter. The Indian delegation that visited 
Iraq was, however, informed by Iraqi authorities that, according to their  
48 

[23 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
definition, diey do not count sand particles under foreign matter. In other words, 
inorganic matter, which is a part and parcel of foreign matter like sand, stones, 
pebbles clay particles etc. are not accepted under this category. The explanation 
given by diem was that only organic foreign matter (like chaff, glumes,weed seeds 
and other edible and inedible grains) are taken under this category. The exporters did 
not know tins position. They presumed tiiat, as in the CODEX standards, die 2% 
foreign matter would include upto 0.5% inorganic matter. The delegation was further 
informed uiat die Iraqi flour mills were not having adequate facilities for separation of 
inorganic matter because of die problem of spare parts required for maintenance of 
such machines owing to UN sanctions. The delegation was further informed that Iraq 
had also rejected die wheat sourced from various other countries on die same grounds. 
As die consignment conformed to die CODEX standards, it was accepted in 
Dubai.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM 
CHAUHAN): (a) and (b) The State-wise exact quantum of foodgrain losses during 
post harvest period at farm level due to insects, rodents, moisture, birds, micro-
organisms, etc. including State of Punjab, Haryana and Madhya Pradesh is not 
known. However, a Committee headed by Dr. V.G. Panse, in its report submiued in 
1968 had estimated annual post harvest losses in the foodgrains in various stages at 
9.33%. These included losses during threshing 
54 

[23 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(1.68%), transportation (0.15%), processing (0.92%), rodents (2.50%), birds

losses were estimated at about 2.7%.

period, the Government of India is operating the Save Grain Campaign (SGC) 
scheme since 1969-70. The main thrust of activities of this scheme are training,

Restrengthening relationship with border countries 
3406. SHRI W. ANGOU SINGH: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL

to (c) Sir, a statement is placed on the Table of the House. 
(a) It is the persistent policy of the Government of India to have cordial and 
peaceful relations with all the neighbouring countries. Government have all along 
striven to develop and strengthen mutually beneficial relations with countries 
bordering India. Government's efforts in this direction in respect of individual 
countries are detailed below: 
82 

[23 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(i) Pakistan: 
India has always endeavoured to establish a relationship of peace, 
friendship and cooperation with Pakistan. For this purpose, in 1998, India initiated the 
Composite Dialogue, which seeks to build trust and confidence, establish a stable 
structure of cooperation and address outstanding issues. In February, 1999, Prime 
Minister Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee visited Lahore, where India's commitment to 
establish such a relationship was reaffirmed. Recently, in keeping with our traditional 
approaches towards Pakist an, on 24th May 2001, Prime Minister extended an 
invitation to the President of Pakistan, General Pervez Musharraf, to visit India. 
Prior to the visit of President Musharraf, Government announced several 
significant confidence building measures, pertaining to peace and security, 
humanitarian issues, promotion of people-to-people contact and trade, which when 
implemented will contribute to the development of good neighbourly ties. The 
visit of the Pakistan President from 14 to 16 July 2001 marked the resumption of 
the dialogue process with Pakistan. Government have reaffirmed their 
commitment to continue with the dialogue process. 
(ii) China: 
Government of India are committed to the development of friendly and 
good nieghbourly relations with China on the basis of the principles of 
Panchsheel and mutual sensitivity to each others concerns. This has been 
underscored during recent high level political exchanges between India and China, 
including during the visit of senior Chinese leader and NPC Chairman Mr. Li Peng 
in January 2001 and the visit of Deputy Chairperson of the Rajya Sabha, Smt. 
Najma Heptulla to China in July 2001. 
India and China seek a fair, r easonable and mutually acceptable 
settlement of the boundary question through peaceful consultation. India & China 
have signed an agreement on the Maintenance of Peace and Tranquility along the 
Line of Actual Control in the India-China Border Areas in 1993 and a second 
agreement on Confidence Building Measures in the Military Field along the Line 
of Actual Control in the India-China Border Areas in 1996. These two 
Agreements provide an institutional framework for the maintenance of peace 
and tranquility in the border areas. Both sides have also agreed to expedite the 
process of LAC clarification within existing mechanisms. 
Bilateral trade between India and China has been steadily expanding In the 
year 2000, two-way trade was USS 2.92 billion, an increase of 47% 
83 

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2001 ] 
over the previous year. As per Chinese statistics, in the first six months of 
year 2001, bilateral trade has reached USS 1.79 billion, an increase of 36.5% 
over the same period last year. Both sides are making efforts to further expand 
trade and economic cooperation. 
There has also been a diversificati on of exchanges in the fields of 
education, culture, science & technology, information technology, labour, etc.

India and Nepal have always shared an intimate relationship with

Bhutan is one of our closest neighbours with which our relationship has

being intensified in diverse areas w ith an emphasis on economic linkages 
following the operationalisation of the India-Sri Lanka Free Trade Agreement 
in March 2001.

India and Maldives enjoy close and cordial relations. The warmth of 
these relations have been kept up through regular exchange of high-level visits 
between the two countries. India have been assisting the Maldives in its 
developmental efforts especially in th e areas of human resource development 
and public health.

Simputer for Poor People 
3440. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India has developed "Simputer", a low cost 
alternative to PC for the first time in the world; 
(b) if so, the salient features of "Simputer" and how is it going to help the poor 
people; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken by his Ministry to penetrate into the village? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (SHRI PRAMOD 
MAHAJAN): (a) and (b) Simputer is low cost hand held computing device with in-
built multiple connectivity options. It is modular and based on Linux Operating 
System, The Simputer has been developed by some Faculty Members of the 
Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore, and a commercial company called Encore 
Software Ltd. It's cost is estimated to be US $ 200 (Rs. 9,000/-) when produced in 
large volumes. It speaks (using Text to Speach) in several Indian Languages and 
uses the Smart Card technology, allowing it to be shared within a community or 
village, lent by a shopkeeper or an office on rental basis. Pro-poor applications such 
as micro banking, metre reading, inventory records etc. are envisaged to be 
possible at an affordable price. Similar systems with some comparable features 
and performance are being developed elsewhere in the world as well. Development 
112 

[23 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
of Simputer in India at present is at the level of Beta prototype testing. 
(c) The Ministry of IT is considering steps to ensure protection of the 
invention/intellectual property in terms of Trade Mark, Patent or copyrights. The MIT 
is also proposing to consider the Simputer and a similar low-cost computer (as a Janata 
PC), as the hardware "engines" providing indigenously developed devices for 
addressing the digital divide.

3472. DR. Y. LAKSHMI PRASAD : Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the action plan to stabilize population growth; 
(b) whether any agency is monitoring the population control action 
plan by the States; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof/ 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (c) After the adoption of National Population Policy 
2000, the long-term objective of which is to achieve a stable population by 
2045, the National Commission on Population requested the States to 
formulate State Population Policies to e ffectively deal with  various issues 
relating to population stabilization in each State. In view of the wide inter-
State and intra-State differences, the St ates were also advised to prepare 
District Action Plans for the identified high fertility districts for improving the 
socio-economic and demographic indicators affecting population growth. In 
addition, the reproductive and child health programmes of the Department of 
Family Welfare and Externally Aided projects in some States are based on the 
Annual Action Plans prepared at the district and State level. Though the 
implementation/monitoring of the State Population Policies is mainly the 
responsibility of the respective State Governments, the monitoring of 
138

the achievement of National Socio-Demographic goals indicated in the National 
Population Policy 2000 remain the concern of the Union Government and the National 
Commission on Population of which all the Chief Ministers are also Members.

Meeting of National Commission on Population 
3475. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAI AH: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a meeting of the National Commission on Popualtion was 
held in New Delhi on 11th April, 2001 under the chairmanship of the Deputy 
Chairman of Planning Commission; 
(b) if so, the main objective for calling the meeting; 
(c) the details of the participants and the response of the States to the 
meeting; and 
(d) the details of the decisions taken at the meeting and their 
implications? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
ARUN SHOURIE): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The National Commission on Population convened a meeting of the 
District Magistrates of 133 high fertility  districts to und erstand the ground 
realities in these districts and to sensitize the District Administrations about the 
various issues which have a bearing on population growth. 
(c) Apart from the District Magistrate s, the meeting presided over by 
Vice-Chairman, NCP was attended by Members of the Planning Commission, 
some Members of the National Commission on Population, senior officials 
from Central Departments, representatives of NGOs and few experts and 
demographers. There was good response from the concerned State 
Governments to the meeting. 
142 

[23 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) After detailed discussions, the District Magistrates resolved to bring up 
population related issues upfront and to fully meet the unmet needs for reproductive 
and child health services so as to reach the replacement level fertility at the earliest. 
They further decided that District Action Plans would be prepared with short-term, 
medium-term and long-term objectives. The action plans prepared/being prepared 
will bring out the position about the infrastructure, human and other resources 
available and the existing gaps in them with a definite programme of action for 
covering these gaps within a given time frame. The implementation of the District 
Action Plans will help imporve the various social, economic and demographic 
indicators in the districts.

Safeguard and protection of women against harassment - 
Amendment of IPC 
SHRIMATI JAYAPRADA NAHATA (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, my 
Special Mention is regarding safety  and protection of women against 
harassment -amendment of IPC.   With a view to safeguarding the 
women, the Andhra 
179 

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2001]  
Pradesh Government passed a Bill, No.8/2000, seeking amendment to 
Section 498A, which deals with the harassment of wife by her husband 
and his relatives. 
A woman can be subjected to cruelty by any wilful conduct or 
by harassing and coercing her to meet certain unlawful demands like 
property, valuable security, money etc. Failure to meet such a demand 
by a woman can result in physical/ mental assault on her. She can be 
hurt/injured, posing danger to her life, limb or health. Such 
circumstances can also force her to commit suicide. 
In this situation, the culprit, i.e. husband or any of his relatives, 
shall be punished with an imprisonment up to three years and shall 
also be fined as contemplated in  Section 498A of the Indian Penal 
Code. 
The Bill of August 2000 of the AP Government specifies that if 
the cruelty is proved, the concerned person should be punishable and 
the offence must be made comp oundable by inserting suitable 
amendment to Section 320 of IPC. 
Similarly,   in   the   above   Bill,    a   provision   has   been   
made for increasing the minimum ma intenance allowance for wife,  
payable by the husband, under Section 125 of Cr.PC, to Rs.3,000/- per 
month from the existing provision of Rs.500/- per month. 
As the matter is pending approval since the last ten months, I 
request the Government of India to take appropriate action, considering 
the importance and the urgency of  helping distressed women in the 
country.

THE CONSTITUTION (NINETY-FIRST AMENDMENT) BILL, 2000 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY 
AFFAIRS AND THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING (SHRI ARUN 
JAITLEY): Madam Deputy Chairman, I move: 
"That the Bill further to amend the Constitution of India, 
as passed by the Lok Sabha, be taken into 
consideration." 
The Forty-Second amendment to the Constitution fixed the 
number of seats and the basis for determining the number of seats 
both in the Lok Sabha and in the State Assemblies. They also fixed 
the basis of the 1971 Census, for the purpose of future delimitation. 
The Constitution amendment 
194 

[23 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
also provided that that  system would continue till such time, till the 
figures of the 2001 Census were act ually available. Therefore, since 
1977, all elections in the country have been held on the basis of the 
number of seats which were fixed on the basis of the 1971 Census; 
and the delimitation of constituencies was done on the basis of the 
1971 Census. That period was over in 2000. Therefore, this hon. 
House has now an obligation to provide an arrangement for the future. 
The Government had introduced the Constitution (Ninety-first 
Amendment) Bill in Parliament. This Bill went to the Parliamentary 
Standing Committee for consideration. I am extremely grateful to the 
Chairman, Shri Pranab Mukherjee and Members of the Committee 
who have examined this issue at length and were able to evolve a 
broad consensus. On this basis, I would request the House to 
consider and pass this Constitution Amendment Bill. 
There are six different articles  of the Constitution which are 
sought to be amended. Article 55 deals with the Presidential election. 
The basis of determination of populat ion there too has to be changed 
from the figure 2000 to 2026. Article 81 deals with the number of seats 
in the Lok Sabha. For this, two different criteria have been adopted. 
For the purpose of fixation of th e number of seats, the 1971 Census 
has been taken into account. The number of seats have been 
determined on the basis of the 1971 Census which are existing today. 
These are sought to be frozen both at the national level as well as at 
the State level. This was consider ed necessary because this freezing 
has been extended till the year 2026.  For various reasons, it found 
favour with the Standing Committee, which the Government has also 
accepted. The first reason was that under the National Population 
Policy, the year 2026 is anticipated to be the year when we shall 
probably attempt to achieve the population stabilisation target. That is 
why the freeze continues till the year 2026. 
The second reason is that there are a number of States which 
have successfully implemented t he Family Planning Programme. 
There are some States which have  not been so successful in 
implementing the Family Planning Programme. If this freeze is not 
imposed, then, the States which hav e successfully implemented the 
Family Planning Programme , actually, their representation in 
Parliament would go down; and those States which have actually 
defaulted in the implementation of the Family Planning Programme, 
would have an incentive because their representation would go up. 
Therefore, in order to remove su ch an anomalous situation, it has 
been considered necessary to freeze the number of seats on the basis 
of the 
195 

RAJYA SABHA [23 A ugust. 2001] 
1971 Census as they existed today, till the year 2026, both, as far as the 
Centre is concerned, and, as far as the States are concerned. However, 
since 1971, it has been noticed that disparities in the size of the number of 
seats and disparities in the size and strength of these seats have grown. 
The seats have become uneven because of the population growth and 
urbanisation. As far as the parliamentary seats are concerned, those figures 
have become uneven. Therefore, a delimitation is required with regard to the 
parliamentary seats, even when the figure remains the same in every State. 
For that delimitation, the Census figure which has been considered relevant 
is the 1991 Census. We are still relying on 1991 Census and not on the 2001 
Census which has been completed, because the figures of the 2001 Census 
are likely to be made available only by the end of the year, 2002. 
Last time, when the Census was conducted, the Delimitation 
Commission was notified in the year 1972 and it took four years to complete 
the exercise. This time, because we are not increasing the number of seats 
but only re-allocating, and also because of more modem technologies being 
available, it is not likely to take four years; it will take much less. But this 
will be a lengthy exercise where various people will have to be heard and 
delimitation will have to be done in each  State. Therefore, it will take a 
reasonable time. If we wait till t he 2002 Census figures are available, 
perhaps, we will not be able to delimit the new constituencies by the time 
the next election normally falls due.  Therefore, for the purpose of 
delimitation, the 1991 Census, which is the last best figure available, has 
been taken as the basis. The same principle which is applicable to the Lok 
Sabha, by amendment of article 82 has been applied to elections, as far as 
State Assemblies are concerned, and the re-adjustment of constituencies is 
also going to be on the same basis. That is, the number of constituencies 
will be as per the 1971 Census, but the re-adjustment of constituencies will 
be on the basis of the 1991 Census, to make them broadly all equal. After 
the Constitution Amendment is passed, it may have to be ratified by the 
States, because, under article 55, Constitution amendments have to be 
ratified by half the State Assemblie s. After the ratification is done, a 
Delimitation Act will have to be framed by the Parliament, where guidelines 
would have to be given as to the basis on which the delimitation would take 
place and the body which will undertake the delimitation exercise. 
There is another significant article which is sought to be amended. 
The   original   Constitution   itself,   under  article   330,   provides   that   the 
196 

[23 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
reservation of the number of seats for the Scheduled Castes and 
Scheduled Tribes constituencies will be on the ba sis of the population 
percentage of these communities. That population percentage was on 
the basis of the 1971 Census. 
Therefore, two amendments ar e consequently necessary to 
the provisions of articles in the Constitution, on that basis. 
With these observations, I co mmend to the hon. House that 
this Bill to amend the Constituti on of India be taken up for 
consideration and be approved by the hon. House. 
The question was proposed.

onwards, there is a specific provision with regard to delimitation of 
constituencies both in Uttar Pradesh and Uttaranchal. In the case of 
Uttaranchal -- since the number of constituencies has increased now 
to 70 -- I understand, the process of  delimitation has already started. 
The process has already started, under  the present law, as it exists 
today. The present law, as it exis ts today, refers to the 1971 Census 
as the basis. It may be likely that by the time it is completed, we may 
have the new Constitution amendment in force. If we are confronted 
with that situation, there is a specific provision for removal of 
difficulties, in the U.P. Reorgani sation Act, and appropriate measures 
will be taken to make sure that t hat process is not disrupted and is 
taken to its logical conclusion, in accordance with the law. 
224 

[23 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
Some hon. Members wanted to know the exact number of 
seats that would be increased in the case of SC/ST. This is not a new 
provision that we are adding. This is  a provision which is existing in 
the present Constitution, under article 330 which says that the number 
of seats to be reserved for the SC /STs will be in proportion to the 
population. And, once the seats are fi xed in accordance with the 1991 
Census -- which is made the basis here -- that is an exercise which 
the Delimitation Commission will itself have to undertake; the 
approximate figure mentioned here is six or seven. But the exact 
figure, and the States where this in crease will take place -- I have got 
the figures of the 1991 increase -- would be known only after the 
Delimitation Commission completes its exercise. In some States, in 
fact, there is a reduction in population. In some States, there is an 
increase in the population, and large part of the increase is confined to 
those areas where a number of new castes have been added to the 
list of the SC/ST. That is the basis for it. But the exac t figure will be 
known only when the Delimitation Commission undertakes that entire 
exercise. Some hon. Mem bers also raised a questi on 'the Bill in itself 
is not complete. What is the basis on which the delimitation would be 
done? Who would do the delimitation?' Madam, this House will have 
an opportunity to consider the De limitation Bill when it is brought 
before the House. All those detai ls would be mentioned in the 
Delimitation Bill itself. A Commission would be constituted. What is the 
composition of the Commission, w ho are the personnel, how are the 
political parties of different regi ons going to be involved in that 
process, is an exercise which w ill be dealt by a specific legislation 
which is going to be passed. A question was also raised as to how we 
are linking it to the family planning programmes. Well, I had made a 
brief statement with regard to this in my opening remarks, where I had 
stated that the rationale behind freezing the seats at the level at which 
they were fixed in 1976 was essentially this. There are a number of 
States which have been able to stabilize the population growth. Now, if 
those States are confronted with a situation that because they are 
achieving the population stabilisation target, their representation in 
Parliament will come down, it is likely to become a disincentive for 
those States which are successfully implementing the family planning 
programmes. Similarly, the States which do not implement the family 
planning programmes successfully, will find that as a result of their 
failure to implement ttie programmes, their representation in the Lok 
Sabha is going to be increased. Ther efore, this rationale should not 
prevail and this policy should not deter the implementation of the 
family planning programmes.  So, irrespective of whether your 
population is stable, 
225 

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2001]  
increasing or decreasing, the number of seats would be fixed. And the 
reason why 2026 has been chosen as the target date is that this is the 
anticipatory date the experts have fixed in the National Population 
Policy. 
Now, whether we are able to achieve this or not will depend 
on how the Central Government perf orms; how the State Government 
performs; or, how the various family planning schemes are 
implemented. But that is the target date. What will happen in case we 
fail? This question has been raised by atleast two Members. Mr, 
Nayyar has also raised the point; are you not going a bit too far. by 
fixing it as 2026? We are now, therefore, effectively binding five 
different Houses which are, in norma l course, likely to be constituted if 
elections are held every five years. Well, we are taking a conscious 
decision with regard to the target date of 2026. But even if the State 
achieves those targets and if both Houses of Parliament want to 
change the date, at any stage, or, for that matter, at a later stage, even 
if this House wants to reconsider the question of delimitation of 
constituencies, for which we are taking the 1991 Census as the basis, 
once the 2011 figures are available or  the 2021 figures are available, 
for those Houses, at that time, it will always be open to reconsider 
those issues, but, at present, the general consensus that has emerged 
from the Standing Committees is that 2026 should be fixed as the 
target date. Just two or three more questions I would like to answer. 
So far as the point of rotation principle is concerned, this issue is not 
covered by this amendment. Ther efore, the Standing Committee did 
not go into this, question. It is not covered by this issue. If at all it ever 
arises, it will have to be taken up separately. Again, a comment was 
made as to why, instead of going to the 2001 Census, we are going 
back to the 1991 Census. As I explained, last time, the process of 
delimitation took four years to be completed. The Delimitation 
Commission was constituted in 1972. It finished its exercise in 1976. 
This time it is expected to be done much earlier, essentially, because 
of the availability of new technologies, that is, computers, etc. And also 
because the exercise is likely to be  smaller, the number of seats not 
being increased. But it is still a fo rmidable exercise. I have consulted 
the experts and they feel, it will still take some time.the earliest date by 
which the Census figures are going to be officially available is the very 
end of 2002. Therefore, if we start by the very end of 2002, even if it is 
available --it may spill into 2004 -- the Members of Lok Sabha and the 
State Assemblies would perhaps, not  know till a few days before the 
elections as to which constituency  and what is the shape of that 
Constituency going to 
226 

[23 August, 2001]  RAJYA SABHA  
be. Therefore, there was a consensu s that instead of going into that 
area of uncertainty, it would be bette r, for the present, to stick to the 
1991 Census figures that are avail able and the delimitation exercise 
can be started immediately. Mr. Nayyar has raised, one point. In fact, 
some other experts have also raised this question. He has even 
written an article to that effect. On account of the Population 
Stabilisation Programme, you are now freezing the number of seats for 
each State so that one State which defaults does not get a 
comparative benefit or advantage over  another State. But he has also 
asked that within the State, why d on't you permit the number of seats 
for the Assembly to be increased. This is a question which he had 
raised;in fact, in the Standing Committee also, a note was circulated 
by him. I have gone through the proceedings of the Standing 
Committee. When it was considered, in 1976, and even earlier, on 
both occasions, the same logic had been applied to the Lok Sabha 
seats as also to the State Assembly  seats. If the population of a State 
is increasing, don't give it the advant age of increase in the number of 
seats, as far as the State itself is concerned, and when this view was 
considered, this was the exact response which the Standing 
Committee, through its Chairman, had to this particular query, that the 
past practice has been that when we are freezing it, we are freezing it 
for both, and also, additionally, we do not want any kind of an incentive 
given to the State to increase the number of seats merely because the 
State is not able to implement the Population Stabilisation programme. 
Madam, I have tried to respond to a number of points which have been 
raised by the hon. members. I am  extremely grateful to them for 
having supported this particular l egislation. I propose to the hon. 
House that this Constitution (A mendment) Bill be approved by the 
House.

THE CODE OF CRIMINAL PROCEDURE (AMENDMENT) BILL. 2001 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI T.N. CHATURVEDI) in the Chair] 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI T.N. CHATURVEDI) : Now, Shri 
Arun Jaitley to move the motion for consideration of the Code of 
Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 2001. 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
AND MINISTER OF SHIPPING (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY):  Sir, I beg to 
move: 
" That the Bill further to amend the Code of Criminal Procedure, 
1973, be taken into consideration." 
Sir, this particular amendment to the Code of Criminal 
Procedure is sought to be introduced into the provisions of section 
125 of the Cr.P.C. 
248 

[23 August, 2001] RAJ YA SABHA 
There are several crucial amendments which are being made to this 
provision. This was a provision whic h was incorporated in the Code of 
Criminal Procedure for the protec tion of those family members who 
are otherwise unable to maintain themselves, namely, wives, children 
and aged parents. In the year 1955, the maximum amount that could 
be paid to them was fixed and that amount was Rs.500. In 1973, when 
we incorporated the new Cr.P.C, we continued with the same amount. 
So, this amount has been continued for more than 45 years. On 
account of the increase in the cost of living there have been repeated 
demands and suggestions that the amount be increased. In fact, the 
Law Commission, at one stage, had suggested that this amount be 
increased to Rs.5,000. The Government took those factors into 
consideration and took an opinion that since it had to be fixed by 
judicial orders, it must be in cons onance with the requirements of the 
wives, children and aged parents as also the paying capacity of the 
husband or the son or the father, as the case may be, there was no 
need to maintain that cap of Rs.500. Therefore, that cap of Rs.500 is 
sought to be removed. 
The other amendment is that there was an ambiguity whether 
there was a provision for payment of interim maintenance under this 
provision or not, the judicial opinion, at some stage recently, was that 
the interim directions were also being passed. But that has been 
clarified by a specific amendment that the interim maintenance can 
also be paid under these provisions. Just as we approved the 
Marriage Laws (Amendment) Bill, ye sterday, there is a corresponding 
amendment in this Bill also that the interim maintenance amount be 
directed to be paid, as far as possible, within a period of 60 days from 
the service of the notice of the application to a person who is liable to 
pay this amount. There is also a cl arificatory amendment to the effect 
that the maintenance would not only cover the maintenance amount 
but also the expenses of the proceedings themselves. There are 
corresponding changes which are suggested to sections 127 and 128 
on account of these amendments. 
I  propose to this august  Hous e that this Bill be taken up for 
consideration and be passed. 
The question was proposed.

PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARATI RAY (West Bengal): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, I appreciate the Bill that has come before the House. I 
must thank the hon. Law Minister  for bringing a progressive 
legislation. Since he has brought this Bill showing concern for the 
helpless wives, children and aged parents, which is important, I want 
to suggest some amendments. The first point is that the concept of 
shared household is very important. It seeks to prevent women, 
dependent parents and children from being dispossessed from their 
shelter and from domestic violence. A provision should be made so 
that the wives and their dependent pa rents and children can stay in 
the marital home or house which they shared together and cannot be 
thrown out. If they are thrown out, they can be put back.   That right 
should be there.   This is one point. 
The second point is that a man can always understate his 
income. A wife often does not know the amount of her husband's 
earnings. 
t 
Therefore, while deciding the amount of maintenance, the 
husband's lifestyle should also be taken into account. The third and 
the most important point which I would like to make is that, there 
should also be an easy way of recovering the amount of maintenance, 
because the husband often evades orders, and another legal suit will 
be necessary to force him to pay t he maintenance. I suggest that a 
mechanism for attachment of his salary should be there. This would 
make it easier for the complainant to get the compensation. With these 
words, I conclude. Thank you.

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2001]  
It has been our experience that when a woman files an 
application in a court for maintenance, she has to wait for years 
together for getting relief from the Court. She is put to a great mental 
agony and financial difficulty till the court grants her some allowance. 
Keeping the difficulties of women in view, the Government has come 
forward with this amendment. 
The objective of the amendment is to ask the husband, who is 
an earning member of the family, to share certain amount or pay 
certain amount to his wife and children who are dependent on him. 
This section was introduced to ensure minimum social security to the 
dependents. The cost of living is increasing day be day. Keeping in 
view the rising cost of living, now it is proposed that the Magistrate can 
order payment of a reasonable interim maintenance allowance and 
expenses on court proceedings. 
The court's order would come within 60 days of the notice. In 
order to achieve the objective, this clause further contemplates that a 
minimum amount of Rs. 500/- can be granted towards maintenance by 
the courts. As a matter of practice, since the Act contemplates Rs. 
500/- most of the courts are awarding less than Rs. 500/- and 
sometimes even less than half the amount. So, the dependents are 
facing a lot of hardships. Now the ceiling is being removed and the 
courts are being given a free hand to award suitable amount towards 
maintenance.  It is a welcome step. 
I would like to make one or two suggestions. This law should 
be amended further. If an appeal is filed, the same should be 
entertained only on payment of 50 per cent of the amount awarded 
and no Appellate Court should grant a stay till 50 per cent of the 
awarded amount is deposited. It will also be advisable to put a time 
limit for disposal of applications filed under section 125 o1 the Criminal 
Procedure Code. The trial courts should be made accountable to the 
concerned portfolio judge of the High Court in case the trial court fails 
to dispose of the application within the stipulated time. 
I would like to appeal to the Government to amend various 
provisions relating to matrimonial disputes. There is a need to adopt a 
comprehensive approach towards matrimonial problems. 
Failure of marriages should not be viewed as a problem of 
individuals but it should be treated as a problem of the society at large. 
Thank you.

judge-made laws abroad, the whole concept of matrimonial house is

Supreme Court said that the right to residence is also a part of 
maintenance, and therefore, when you award maintenance, keep in 
mind that it is not merely for the food or the clothing of the lady that it is 
required, but the right to residence is  also a part of the maintenance. 
Therefore, there is a large distance that we have to cover in bringing 
our laws, particularly, civil laws a nd personal laws, at par with what 
they should be in an ideal situation.  Yesterday, in the course of the 
discussion on the other Bill, a question was raised that there are 
several cases where actual incomes are concealed, and where actual 
incomes are concealed, our judges, who interpret those laws and pass 
orders, are all expected that they have already developed the whole lot 
of defence.... and they do not conf ine themselves merely to the 
certificates which are placed before them but they also look beyond 
the certificates, as to the requi rement, the life-style and the other 
relevant factors which are required for the purposes of this law itself. 
Sir, this is a specific law we are dealing with, Section 125. I wish, as 
we always do suggest in the course  of discussions, that there should 
be comprehensive legislations. But comprehensive legislations which 
will resolve and solve all problems are, probably, still a far cry, and, 
therefore, while we must take all these suggestions into account and 
look forward those comprehensive legislations

or, at least, certain specific legislat ions which, step by  step, will also 
aid these rights which we are trying to strengthen, but it is equally 
important that what appears to us today to be inadequacies in our law 
or aberrations in our law are suitab ly checked so that the rights could 
be strengthened. 
One great advantage of Section 125 would be that whereas in 
all civil laws and personal laws except with regard to the Adoption and 
Maintenance Act, there had to be a matrimonial dispute. The 
matrimonial dispute could be in relation to a divorce case, in relation to 
restoration of conjugal rights or a matrimonial dispute in which the 
judge would get jurisdiction to pass an interim order or a final order 
with regard to the maintenance. Therefore, there must be some 
element of discard between the wife  and the husband, in which the 
jurisdiction to pass these interim orders would arise, and they would 
become final orders after the matrimonial proceeding is disposed of. 
Section 125 is, however, different. This was a law to make sure that 
any section of society, particular ly the three specified sections-the 
aged parents, the young children and the wives--are not driven to any 
form of destitution by the earning hand who is expected to support 
them, and thjs^aming hand must be compelled to prevent any form of 
starvation ano^-anyform of destitution, and this was an assistance not 
arising out of any personal law provisions, but arising out of the 
criminal law provisions where under  the Criminal Procedure Code, a 
magistrate would have the power. So , in one sense, section 125 is 
different like its predecessor sections 488 where there need not be a 
matrimonial dispute, there need not be a divorce petition, there need 
not be any other petition of discard between the wife and the husband. 
The wife and the husband may be actually living together, maybe, with 
strained relations. The parents may be living with the son. But in case 
they felt that they were not being adequately maintained, all that they 
had to do was to go to the nearest magistrate. They do not have to go 
to the district courts because in te hsils you find even the district courts 
are at a reasonable distance. They could go to the nearest magistrate 
within whose jurisdiction they reside . All that they are required to do is 
a two-page application saying, "We have no resources. The man's life-
style is this, his earnings are this." And the magistrate would pass 
orders in support of the wife, ch ildren and parents. The difficulty, 
however, arose that the cost of livi ng increased, and for the last 46 
years we pegged this amount at an outer limit of Rs.500/-. This 
Rs.500/- was considered inadequate, and since the magistrate has no 
jurisdiction to award any amount beyond Rs.500/-, people started,

Some other suggestions have been made. Even though 
maintenance covers residence, I think, at some stage, we will require a 
larger debate in this House. We have also studied the personal laws 
and the family laws elsewhere in the world. There are orders of

passed in relation to the right to live in a residence. There may be

But the law should move forward, by including in its ambit all the 
directions which are required. Mr. Je thmalani has suggested that this 
being a penal law provision, with a provision for appeal, we do hope 
and we do expect our judges, who are a judicially trained mind, and 
the higher courts would lay down strict guidelines in this regard and
